DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
This study asks Cabinet to approve district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households. It puts the net cost at £490,000 a year, covered by a provisional £520,000 new-burdens grant.

The pilot is a good basis and the cost arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. But Table 1 contradicts the study's central claim, the tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot, and the treatment plant can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage. Once these are corrected, the net cost most likely exceeds the funding, before several missing cost lines are added.

## 1. Participation was not similar across houses and flats

- Houses participated at **66%**, flats at **21%**. Flats participated at less than a third of the rate of houses.
- "Broadly similar across housing types" is therefore wrong, and so is the recommendation it supports: a single uniform service with no separate approach for flats. The pilot actually shows that flats need a different approach, for example communal bins, different caddies or targeted engagement.
- The author's description repeats the error ("participation held up across houses and flats").

## 2. The projection uses a 64% rate that isn't in the pilot

- The pilot's overall participation was **57%**, not 64%. The 64% matches neither houses (66%) nor the overall figure.
- The pilot was 20% flats, the same as the district, so the overall pilot rate already reflects the district's mix. Calculating each housing type separately gives the same answer:
  - Houses: 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg × 52 ≈ **2,713 t**
  - Flats: 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg × 52 ≈ **159 t**
  - **Total ≈ 2,870 t a year**, not 3,290 t. That is about 13% lower.
- The study's arithmetic using 64% is correct (≈3,288 t). The problem is the input.

## 3. The treatment plant can't take the projected tonnage

- Brookfield can take only **1,800 t a year until 2029**. Even the corrected 2,870 t is about **1,070 t over** that limit.
- The rest would go to the plant **46 miles away**, at a gate fee the study doesn't give, plus extra haulage. It may also need a transfer station.
- "Treatment is local" is therefore true for only about 60% of the tonnage.

## 4. The disposal saving and funding position

The £74 saving per tonne applies in full only to tonnage Brookfield accepts:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k funding |
|---|---|---|---|
| As in study (3,290 t, all Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | £30k headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, ignoring the Brookfield cap (2,870 t) | £212,000 | £521,000 | ~£1k short |
| 1,800 t to Brookfield; rest to second plant at Brookfield's fee, no extra haulage | £212,000 | £521,000+ | short, plus haulage |
| 1,800 t to Brookfield; no saving on the rest | £133,000 | £600,000 | ~£80k short |

The realistic range is **roughly £520,000 to £600,000 a year**, against provisional funding of £520,000, before the missing costs below.

**Who gets the disposal saving?** Thornbury is a *district* council. In two-tier areas, the county council usually pays for disposal, including incineration. If that applies here, the £112-per-tonne saving lands with the county, not Thornbury, unless there is a recycling-credit or cost-sharing agreement. If there isn't, the district has almost no offsetting saving and the net cost is close to the full £733,000. This needs confirming before the report goes to Cabinet.

## 5. Costs missing from Table 2

The arithmetic in Table 2 is correct (£990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400; total £733,400). But "every cost line shown" isn't accurate. These are missing:

- **Cover for leave and sickness** for 12 operatives. Rounds run every week, so absences need agency or relief staff, typically adding 15–20% to crew costs.
- **A spare vehicle.** With six vehicles all in daily use, a single breakdown means missed collections.
- **Haulage and gate fee** for tonnage sent to the second plant.
- **Supervision, the dedicated phone line and web page, depot space and insurance.**
- **Ongoing liners.** Residents get a three-month supply. If the Council stops providing liners, participation may fall; if it continues, the annual cost should be stated.
- **The basis for the £34,000 per operative:** salary only, or including employer's on-costs? It should also say whether the £990,000 vehicle purchase is funded by capital grant or borrowing. If borrowing, there are financing costs.

## 6. Other points

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households." The 43% who didn't take part are probably under-represented. The study should give the response rate and whether non-participants were surveyed.
- **The timetable is very tight:**
  - Three months from order to delivery is optimistic for specialist food waste vehicles, which often take longer. The supplier's quoted lead time should be included.
  - Vehicle delivery, crew training, and caddy delivery to 52,000 households all fall in March 2027, with collections starting 5 April. If the vehicles are even a few weeks late, the whole start date moves.
- **The statutory deadline:** for most English councils, weekly food waste collection had to start by 31 March 2026. Starting in April 2027, the study should say whether Thornbury has a transitional arrangement. If it doesn't, the report should acknowledge it is late.
- The overall figure of 1.9 kg per participating household is rounded up from 1.86. That's harmless, but the projection by housing type above avoids the issue.

## What should change before this goes to Cabinet

1. Rewrite the housing-type finding and drop the "uniform service" recommendation. Propose a specific approach for flats.
2. Recalculate tonnage from the pilot's actual rates (about 2,870 t).
3. Set out treatment for the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 t cap: the second plant's gate fee, haulage and logistics, through to 2029.
4. Confirm whether the disposal saving belongs to Thornbury or the county.
5. Add the missing cost lines and show the net cost against funding under the scenarios above.
6. Obtain a confirmed vehicle lead time and build in a contingency start date.

The service is required by law, so the question isn't whether to do it. The question is whether Cabinet is told it is fully funded. On the study's own numbers, it probably isn't. Cabinet should approve it knowing about the likely shortfall and with a plan for covering it.
